Do you know what we are doing? Again, I am not going to be drawn away from what I shall designate as purely a little business talk to my friends here, and not a political discussion at all. I put it once more to the house whether or not the net result of increasing the volume is not to reduce the unit cost if you give the opportunity for the increased volume to be sold here. That is all. I have gone into this matter at great length because I want to make perfectly clear the purpose of the legislation that placed a high duty, the highest this country has known, upon agricultural implements. It was done, as I said when standing in the Prime Minister's place over there, for the purpose of giving Canadian producers the market; and it was done with two conditions, one affecting the individual and the other the industry. We made it possible that they could become effective if the situation prevailed for which they provided a remedy. It did in the case of glass, and action was taken immediately by the governor in council. What is more; there was one complaint which I recall with regard to prices, and on investigation it turned out that it had reference to raw material and nothing else. Every time any question arose where it was suggested that there should not be an increase in price, we investigated.
How can we hope to maintain this industry unless we can give it a market? I am not unmindful of the fact that one of these companies has a business in Germany, a factory

in France, a couple of factories in the United States, an interest in the Sunshine works in Australia, and works at Brantford and Toronto; but they are not manufacturing abroad solely to sell here, and the prices of their competitors, if they were able to sell their surplus goods in this country, with our limited production as against their mass production, would be lower than ours, and they would put us out of business. We would fail. That is all there is about it. It is the 125,000,000 beside us as against 11,000,000 here that must be considered; it is the unit cost of mass production as against the unit cost of our limited production.
Take cream separators, to which reference has been made. Do we want a cream separator industry in Canada or not? The hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Duffus) says, "Yes, we need it"; the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr McCann) says so too. Well, if we want this industry we ought to give it a fair opportunity with competition from abroad. May I point out-and it is one of the reasons I rose in my place-that in 1932, when we negotiated the British preference, we asked the British people, when the preference was given, whether or not they could undertake to provide us with cream separators in addition to what we ourselves were producing. The firm of Lister and Company had been providing cream separators for a long time in New Zealand; they supplied half the requirements there-and in New Zealand they make as good butter as anywhere else. The British government took over the plant when the war broke out, and because of that, the United Kingdom shipped to Canada only two separators in 1932. In 1933 there were shipped 535; in 1934, 956; in 1935, 1,355; in 1936, 1,994; in 1937, 3,163. We gave the preference to those producers who were well established in this country and they added to what we ourselves were doing. We believed that it was desirable to maintain the industry, a belief which is indicated by the addresses in this house, and we therefore passed the legislation to which I have directed attention. Is it desirable to do away with that British preference, to deny to this old and established house the preference we gave them in 1932 and for which they paid handsomely? As the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) has made clear in the house, they gave ample compensation for it, and established for our products in their markets a position which more than balanced what we did for them.
As I have pointed out, unless we are prepared to take such action as may be necessary to ensure that volume can be maintained

Farm Implements Committee Report
in Canada we are bound to increase unit costs; and an increase in unit costs means that, without a duty or with a nominal duty, an unfair opportunity will be afforded the country with mass production to compete against us, with our production on a limited scale and with a population of 11,000,000, especially having regard to the fact that over half of our population now find homes in cities and towns rather than in the rural sections as heretofore.
There are other matters to which reference has been made. There is the effect upon our country's economic structure, not with respect to income tax alone but with respect to municipal taxes, provincial taxes, taxes on individuals, and the question of employment, direct and indirect. When I went into the factory in Australia I saw at once that coal was being used in large quantities, and so was coke. That gave employment to the coal mines at Newcastle. I saw at once that there were workmen engaged with wood, and I knew that meant work in the forest and everything connected with the fabrication of wood. I saw steel, and I knew that steel had been manufactured at the plant I had seen a few days before at Newcastle, just as in this country pig iron and steel in Canadian factories gives employment to men in Cape Breton or Hamilton or at the Sault. I realized that all these things combined to create the interdependence of industry, the relationship between the production of the raw material and the production of the manufactured article in its finished form. We must be prepared as men of business to deal with this matter in a purely business way and to provide, not protection for exploitation, but that measure of protection which will ensure equality of opportunity to Canadians with our limited market, in order that they may compete against the mass production of other countries, and that can be brought about only by the methods to which I have directed attention. I suggest that this report, if acted upon, will strike a blow at industry, will increase unemployment, and will render it far more difficult for the government to deal with the complex and difficult problems with which it is faced.
I yield to no man in the desire for cheap agricultural implements for the men who toil on the soil. I have studied this question since I first went to western Canada, and I have no doubt that if the house were prepared, with the legislation which is now on the statute books, to increase unit production in Canada to a point where we might be able with certainty to contemplate a market for Canadian production on the conditions that I have outlined, we would be able to
reduce prices materially, because the unit cost would have been reduced strictly in accordance with increase in volume-and the volume here is so small, with 11,000,000, so insignificant compared with 125,000,000, in the manufacture of machines for use in the cotton fields in the south and in the wheat fields of the north, for use with vegetables and corn, with every kind of production of the farmer, as they are in that great republic, and with unit costs continually being reduced by mass production. What it is proposed to do, as suggested by the hon. member who moved the adoption of this report, would result in lessening the unit production by reason of increased competition for the moment by those engaged in mass production on a scale of which the world has never seen the like.
Let me refer again to what Mr. Fielding said in this house as Minister of Finance when he pointed out the dangers of a people finding their factories closed by competition from abroad. He said: "You will get cheaper goods for the time being, much cheaper; but in the end, when your factories are gone, when your mills are closed, when your countrymen are unemployed, the price will be the price that the monopolist fixes; and you will have no control over him, because you cannot get your Canadians to start again." If any hon. member is interested in reading the history of tariff legislation, he will find in the library many books upon the subject. If the principle my hon. friend contends for had been applied, you would not have what you have in this country to-day, namely, the production of Canadian steel rails for our railways. When I first went west I travelled on rails manufactured in the United Kingdom and in Germany. They bore the mark of Krupp or Barrow and other names. My inquiries-and this is subject to correction-lead me to believe that there is not now a rail on the main line of the Canadian Pacific between Montreal and Vancouver which was not made in Canada. I also believe, although upon this too I speak subject to correction, that the same is true with respect to the Canadian National Railways. Is that not a striking illustration of what I say? We gave them the entire volume of Canadian business. Yet forty years ago practically no rails were produced in Canada.
For that reason I have endeavoured not to enter into a controversy with those who have spoken before me on this question; there will be ample opportunity to controvert what I regard as some mistaken statements which have been made. But I appeal to them to ask themselves whether or not it is doing a service to this country to create an impression which

MOTION FOB CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to one without party prejudice- and I think I can claim that-listening to this discussion there comes a sense of bewilderment and frustration. Here we have had about three or four different points of view expressed; one declares that you must have higher tariff, another that you must keep tariffs where they are, another that tariffs must be lowered and still another that there should be no tariffs at all. In the midst of it the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) rises in his place and gives a very fine, straightforward talk. If we could only be sure that the Minister of Agriculture had the disposition, in the first place-which I rather think he has-and the power, in the second place, to do what he implied in his speech he would do. probably we could breathe more easily; but I am inclined to be afraid that about all we will get out of this situation will be more compromise.
Compromise is a very fine thing, Mr. Speaker, providing one individual does not have to do all the compromising. What has been happening for the last forty years in western Canada, and, I fancy, in other parts of Canada as well where there is agriculture, is this: If you can imagine the agricultural interests starting at one end of a line and industry starting at the other, each of them entitled to fifty per cent of the line, probably there was a time when people tried to give each group the fifty per cent of the line to which it was entitled. But gradually the secondary producers have been claiming sixty, sixty-five, sixty-six, seventy, seventy-five and eighty per cent of the line, while the farmers have been continually pressing for at least fifty per cent. Now, with industry calling for eighty per cent of the line and the farmers claiming fifty per cent, it is not difficult to see about where the compromise is going to fall. Unless something is done very quickly the farmers are going to be "compromised" right out of the picture; that is actually happening at the present time to a very dangerous degree.
I think in what I have to say I shall follow the general outline adopted by the right hon.

leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I thought he made a very fine address just before six o'clock, and I am sure he will be quite pleased to consider the problems of the farmers under exactly the same headings that he used. His first question was something like this: Is it desirable to have an agricultural implement industry in Canada? I am going to grant that it is desirable, but I am going to ask this counter-question: Is it desirable that we should have an agricultural industry in Canada? Just as the right hon. leader of the opposition concluded that everyone would answer yes to his question, so I assume that everyone will certainly answer to mine, Yes it is desirable that Canada should have an agricultural industry. Let us start as members of this parliament on that basis: It is desirable that Canada should have an agricultural industry now and in the future. There are several reasons why that is so. I think it is not necessary to stress them before this house, but it might be well to mention just a few.
In the first place, all secondary industries must recognize that without the farmers their prosperity would be greatly hampered, so that to be able to keep the goose laying the golden eggs it is important that we give the goose at least enough feed to keep her alive. But that is not all. While there is a great tendency for people to move from the country into the city-and that we will all grant- still when they get into the city they must be fed, and they are fed largely from the farm. All the fine observations which the right hon. leader of the opposition made this afternoon were perfectly sound, and I do not question them for one minute. But if in time of national emergency we should find ourselves in an extremely embarrassing position without secondary industries, how much more grievous would be our position if we should find ourselves with a seriously depleted agricultural industry? And that is becoming at the present time not only a possibility but a probability.
While we must be able to find food for the teeming thousands who are increasing in numbers in our cities, yet more and more we must look to a more suitable way of feeding all our people. We in Canada are not commencing to consume the agricultural products which our population should consume. I was much surprised at some facts I found bearing on this question which I am now going to submit to the house, and I think hon. members will find them interesting:
An inquiry instituted in the United States and worked out by dietetic experts and agronomists in the United States Department of Agriculture revealed, with respect to agricultural production, that if every person in the

Farm Implements Committee Report
United States could have a thoroughly adequate diet, it would be necessary to bring under cultivation 40,889,000 acres more than were under cultivation in 1933, or 22,391,000 more than the average under cultivation for the five years, 1928-32. The details of the increased production over the average for 1928-32 that would be necessary, are illuminating; they include: An increase of 76 per cent in dairy cattle; 43 per cent in beef cattle; 68 per cent in veal calves; 22 per cent in hogs; 42 per cent in sheep and lambs; 36 per cent in poultry. It would be necessary to increase the acreage under vegetables by 204 per cent; under citrus fruits and grapes 112 per cent-
That item, of course, would not apply to Canada:

and under small fruits 282 per cent. True, the acreage under wheat in this dietetic plan would he reduced 57 per cent, but that would simply remove the United States completely out of the international market.
Lest it be assumed that the cost of this diet is extremely extravagant we add that it amounts to $12.75 per week for a family of five, statisticians of the United States say that only 21 per cent of the people can afford that amount of food.
I am much afraid, Mr. Speaker, that the conditions obtaining in the United States obtain in equal degree in the Dominion of Canada, and that probably only twenty-one per cent of the population of Canada can afford to have what they need of the agricultural products which we in this country are equipped to produce in profuse abundance. But we are adopting from year to year policies which I am convinced are depleting our agricultural productive power. The statement may sound extreme, but all you need to do to realize its truth is just to travel through our great agricultural areas, where you cannot fail to be impressed by the tremendous number of farms that have been deserted. Why have they been deserted? Last year I had the privilege of travelling through a large part of the splendid province of British Columbia, and I was astounded at the number of fertile fruit farms that were standing idle. I was told by people who knew, that it would not pay even to trim the fruit trees. Why? "No sale," they said; "what's the use?"
What are we doing in Canada? We are destroying those fruit-producing areas as surely as I stand here. "Well," some people may say, "what can we do about it?" Well, we are the government of Canada. Perhaps no more needs to be said.
If the United States needs to increase her ability to consume agricultural products, then surely we need to, as well. But the all important thing, as I see it, before we learn how to enable our people to consume these
products, is to see to it that we do not destroy our ability to produce them, so that we shall have them to consume when we learn how to do so. This is a far more serious matter than I fear the average individual in this country realizes. In the report of the nineteenth session of the International Labour Conference will be found this statement;
The cares of the American, Argentinian, Australian, Canadian or eastern European farmer would be conjured away if the urban populations of Europe and America could eat even a little more bread, butter and meat per head.
We are worrying about overproduction on our farms. There is a suggested solution, although up to the present time, strangely enough, though I have listened with great care, I have not heard advanced in this long debate, which has continued ever since the early part of March, a single constructive idea as to how we can enable our people to consume more except the suggestion from the Conservative party that if you put up a sufficiently high tariff wall you will enable your producers to get the home market. I grant that .there may be some virtue in that suggestion. I shall not discuss it at all now, except to say that the most remarkable thing about it is that if that is the solution, it is strange that our people have been fighting over the question for all these generations and have not yet been able to come to a satisfactory decision about it. That is dismaying! If we must continue through another series of generations before we can decide which of these two policies is the better for Canada, what is going to happen to Canada in the meantime?
Is it desirable that Canada should have an agricultural industry? I have dealt with that from two standpoints. There is a third one. Three provinces of this dominion are primarily agricultural provinces. If we destroy the agricultural industry of this dominion, indisputably we destroy those three provinces. I think that can be said with complete confidence. I know it is not clear to a great many people-it would not have been clear to me if I had not gone into the subject with some care; I should still have thought just as an ordinary citizen-yet the policies in operation to-day are destroying those three provinces economically.
Suppose we grant for the sake of argument and progress that it is desirable to have an agricultural industry in Canada; then I should like to follow the two lines of argument which were pursued by the right hon. leader of the opposition. If they apply to the secondary industries they must apply

Farm Implements Committee Report
with equal force to the primary industry of agriculture. His first statement, as I recall it, was that the quality of the product should be of the best. If there is anything which has desolated my feelings during the last seven or eight years it has been to see, in travelling through the splendid agricultural regions of my home province, to what an alarming degree the quality of production has been falling. I was raised on a farm; my roots are right in the soil, and I know whereof I speak. Where, as recently as 1928, we found it profitable to keep up our fine breeds of cattle, both milking and beef breeds, of swine and poultry and sheep, we no longer find it profitable. It now appears not economically sound to spend the amount of money on breeding stock which years ago we expended, for the reason that there is not a sufficient margin to make it pay. The result is that all over the agricultural areas of this country, at least in the three western provinces, people in general are unable to keep up the standard of quality, although there are exceptions. Generally speaking, the products of the cattle, sheep, horse, swine and poultry producing plants are depreciating rapidly, largely because the owners cannot replenish their breeding stock. That is a serious matter. Furthermore, the equipment is deteriorating. It is a rare experience to pass a farm where they have been able to paint the buildings. All over Canada, I find, it is an uncommon thing to see a farm where a new home or a new barn has been erected. As the hon. member who spoke a few minutes ago said, the farmers generally speaking are "getting by" by every means they can contrive with old machinery which should have been discarded years ago. What does that mean? It means that if we should be plunged into a national calamity comparable with the one which overtook us in 1914, it would be impossible for a considerable length of time for us to reach a parallel degree of production. I believe there can be no satisfying answer to that statement. We are not keeping up the quality.
Then, on a great many farms the land has been allowed to become weedy. Why? Because the farmers are not as good as they were? No; because they simply cannot afford to cultivate the land as they feel it should be cultivated. In many places fertility is decreasing because the farmers are unable to provide fertilizers; they cannot apply the crop rotations which should be employed in order to preserve the land; in many instances they are unable to adopt farming methods which will preserve the soil. So to 
a disquieting degree we are failing to keep up our quality. I am familiar with the exceptions. There will be in a given area three or four, or perhaps five or six such, depending upon the size of the district; but the majority, the great body upon whom we should depend, are not able to stand up to the difficulties.
The next important statement which the leader of the opposition made, and which is perfectly sound, is that price must cover costs, I believe hon. members who have been indulgent enough to listen to the remarks of our group have realized that over and over again we have stressed that your price must cover your costs. In laying down that principle the leader of the opposition was genuinely progressive in his economics. On that score let us examine the position of the agricultural industry. A farmer's costs are fixed. The leader of the opposition said that a manufacturer's costs are fixed. We will grant that. But few people realize that the farmer's costs are more inevitably fixed than those of the manufacturer. Let us examine them for a few moments. The farmer's handling charges must remain permanent. He has nothing to do with transportation charges. Out in the west an attempt has been made to enable trucks to replace other means of transportation; but, unbelievable as it may seem, there has been-a most assiduous movement to impose such licence fees on the trucks as to hamper that means of reducing costs. The farmer's interest.' rates are also fixed, or were until certain provinces began to move in the matter. His taxes' are fixed. The farmer carries in the main the provincial, municipal and also school taxes throughout vast rural areas, and from those charges there is no escape. Everything he buys has the price fixed, but not by him. It matters not how many members he sends to. parliament: they lift their voices as men crying in the wilderness whom people indulgently and with patience abide, but concerning whom nobody ever thinks it necessary to do anything.	.
Consider the manufacturer of this binder of which hon. members have been speaking; does he depend upon supply and demand before he decides what his price is going to' b ? No; he knows in January what the price will be next August, and he manufactures the' number of implements which he thinks will be demanded and can be sold. Contrast that with the situation which faces the farmer. I am not making any charges concerning what has happened in Canada, but this thing has. generally occurred. Manufacturing industries have got together and have agreed upon at

Farm Implements Committee Report
fixed price. This has been brought out time and again by speakers in this debate. I think it was elicited clearly in the investigation. Thus they formed a cartel and they fixed the price.
Now the tariff comes in to help them. Strangely enough, when a tariff question is to be decided, the men who can get close to the powers that be and make their influence felt are the men of wealth, the men who are concentrated. What chance have the farmers, scattered over thousands of miles? Again, their voices are as voices crying in the wilderness, they are scarcely listened to; the result is that the tariffs are set to suit the manufacturers. This painful truth cannot, I think, be questioned. All this debate that we have had during the last few days has tended to show the same thing. We are concerned earnestly about seeing that the Massey-Harris Company recovers its costs, but we are never worried about all the thousands of farmers whether they even survive or not.
It is commonly believed that there is a free market. Many people talk about free markets. I ask hon. members how much freedom there is in the market I have indicated, when these big concerns are able to get together and decide what the prices shall be. How can anyone call that a free market? Some hon. members have suggested in this debate that if we removed the tariff between Canada and the United States it would automatically bring down the prices of implements. I do not argue that; but I notice, from the figures I have of costs across the line, that they have similar troubles there. So, how much good it would do us to remove the tariff entirely, is a debatable matter. Competition among these men does not cut prices; it used to, but they have learned better now. One powerful man in my constituency told me in a conversation years before I was elected that big men do not fight each other. That statement I find has much more meaning than I thought it had when I first heard it. Big men cooperate. Contrast that situation with that of the farmer. The farmer's prices are not protected. If there is any protection it is meagre. I will grant that the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Macdonald) gave us a fine statement with regard to the amount of protection that farmers have. But when you compare the amount of protection that the farmers have on their prices with the protection these "infant industries" of ours have on theirs, you are impressed mainly by the disparity.
The farmer sells his goods in the open market and competition does have something
to do with his prices; the law of supply and demand also undoubtedly has something to do with them. He has no way by which he can limit production and set a price, producing only what he is able to sell at a given figure. When his price begins to go down he does everything in his power to keep his business going and he increases production more and more, with the result that he only aggravates the situation for himself by producing tremendously more than is required, thereby bringing prices down still further. Contrast that with the situation confronting the manufacturer-and remember incidentally that this situation as a whole faces three provinces of this dominion-and then meditate what are the causes of Canada's "stresses and strains". How can the farmers live under such conditions?
There is another matter to which I should like to refer. The farmers' price fluctuates from day to day. Tens of thousands of farmers are virtually ruined because they are compelled by force of circumstances to sell when the prices are down, and they are mortified a few weeks afterwards to find that prices have gone up, which would have doubled their income from a hard year of toil. Someone else has the advantage; they have not. And usually that person is not in any of the three western provinces. I have not spoken very much for the farmers up to the present time, though my constituency is primarily agricultural. If I start talking about farmers' problems I am perfectly at home; the only reason I have not spoken about them before is that I am intent upon a solution rather than upon railing against their ills. When we in parliament have decided that these difficulties do exist, and when we have decided further, as I am sure we have, that something must be done, what do we now do but shrug helpless shoulders and wave helpless hands and say, "I am sure I don't know what to do". There must be a solution. Consequently I have not spoken very much about the inequities and the disabilities under which my constituency suffers. We know all about these. We fancy that the men whom we sent here in previous years told the house all about them.
Lest there should be some people who may be inclined to think that what I am saying is not completely justified-my statement with regard to the way in which the big interests are able to set prices-let me refer to three or four -bits of evidence. Gardiner C. Means of Columbia university in 1935 issued a document which is called Industrial Prices and Their Inflexibility. In this he shows the way in which prices and production varied between

1929 and 1933. His figures are extremely illuminating. I am going to put the figures on Hansard and then talk about them for a few minutes, because, to a large degree, in these figures lies the cause of our woe in Alberta, as well as the woe in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. At least, here lies one of the causes of the trouble in connection with this very question we are now discussing.
There are two columns, " permanent drop in prices " and " permanent drop in production." The first item is agricultural implements, the very item we are discussing to-day. The permanent drop in prices was six per cent, which means that the lowest drop in the prices of agricultural implements in the United States between 1929 and 1933 was six per cent. Contrast that with what happened to farmers' products! Implement production was curtailed or limited or reduced to artificial scarcity eighty per cent. The protection for agriculture is very meagre. If we are going to solve this problem about which we are talking, we must adopt some means designed to achieve the end which President Roosevelt apparently had in mind in his policies under the NRA and the AAA, the object being to bring primary producers' prices into line with secondary production prices. In Canada we have not given protection to our primary producers.

Motions for Papers
I have here a statement of an investigation conducted by the Edmonton chamber of commerce during the last year, which I shall read:
Alberta is handicapped frequently by a tendency under national tariff policy to facilitate the entry of agricultural products of other countries in return for concessions to Canadian manufactured goods.
This tendency is illustrated in the existing trade agreements with Australia and New Zealand, respectively, under which Canada reduced her duty on Australian and New Zealand butter in return for concessions by those two dominions on automobiles, rubber goods, newsprint, lumber, paper, fish and other manufactured goods. Similarly, under the agreement with New Zealand, the duty on mutton was reduced. The free entry of vegetable oils under the trade agreement with the United Kingdom already mentioned above is another illustration of this tendency. Moreover, the variation in duties on agricultural products of these kinds results in serious discouragement to the development of the production in Alberta of dairy and animal products, with a consequent obstacle to the diversification of farm production.

very quickly. The result of the whole thing is that we are simply not doing for agriculture what must be done if we are to maintain a sound economic structure in this dominion. What must we do? I suggest as palliatives, these, mainly drawn from the committee's report: Let us give our farmers protection. If the secondary industries must have protection, surely the farmers must have it also. We must be prepared to give subsidies perhaps. We must reduce the protection to secondary industries to an extent which at least will enable the farmers to live. subtopic: VANCOUVER SITUATION RESPECTING CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE HOMELESS UNEMPLOYED MEN

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour):	Mr. Speaker, on Friday last a
question was put by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) with respect to the position of single unemployed men formerly employed in the forestry conservation camps in British Columbia. I may reply that during the winter months of 1937 and 1938, under a dominion-provincial agreement with British Columbia, some 4,600 men were provided for under these forestry plans. They were paid at the rate of thirty cents an hour, with a deduction for board, and a portion of their pay was deferred and made payable to them after the termination of their service, by vouchers negotiable at the post office. I should mention that, during the same period, in addition to the forestry plan 300 men were given employment in British Columbia on farms. These special plans for dealing with the transient problem in western Canada during the winter months were terminated at the end of April. In dealing with this problem in British Columbia and

in other provinces we have acted and are acting upon the basis of consultation and cooperation with the provincial governments.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

speechtext: Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour) moved the third reading of Bill No. 105, to assist in the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to avail myself of this opportunity to deal with the statement made a few days ago by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) in connection with this measure. I was called out of the house at the time he was speaking, and so I did not deal with his statement at that time.
As reported at page 2527 of Hansard for May 3, I said:
The minister selected a very bad illustration indeed. The Fort Henry work was done under contract, and the contract was let by the provincial government. It is all very well for the minister to say that he asked the provincial government that there should be no discrimination. But the contractor, the Frid Construction Company if I remember aright, bad as one of its officers, according to the letterhead I have, the president of the Kingston Liberal Association. And in answers to questions put upon the order paper, not one, two or three, but many of them, we have it indicated that men were given employment on the recommendation of that very man. Those were men who had no more claim upon employment than others unemployed. They were not selected by their names being taken out of a hat; they were not called; but this man sends a letter and on the strength of it we are told by the return filed in this house-not veiled insinuations of the leader of the opposition-that these men went down to Trenton and other places and were given their positions on the recommendation of that man.
Mr. Rogers: At Trenton, does my right hon. friend say ?
Mr. Bennett:	I think Trenton was one of
the places.
Mr. Rogers: But this was not relief work.
Mr. Bennett: Oh, then there is a distinction between the two?
Mr. Rogers:	Certainly there is.
I said, "if I remember correctly,"; I did not have my papers with me. But I immediately got them when I went upstairs, and had I been in the house when the hon. member was speaking I would have at once answered his question. As reported at page 1846 of Hansard for March 30, 1938, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Clarke) asked

Relief and Agricultural Distress
whether Mr. Robinson was employed as a carpenter at the signal corps, Barriefield, under the Department of National Defence, and also on whose recommendation he was employed, together with two other questions. The answer was that he was employed on the recommendation of Mr. A. E. Stansbury.
The same hon. member asked a similar question with respect to Roy Graham, and the answer was "Mr. A. E. Stansbury." He asked the same question with respect to William Fowler, and the answer was "Recommended by Ontario Employment Agency."
The hon. member for Rosedale asked with respect to where this camp is located, and the answer was that it was situated in Frontenac-Addington. He asked a similar question with respect to Henry Bearance, and the answer was that it was on the recommendation of A. E. Stansbury. Then, there is a question at the top of page 1847 with respect to Mr. John Doyle, asked by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross), and the answer was that it was on the recommendation of Mr. A. E. Stansbury; and the same with respect to Mr. Harold Johnston.
I said that I had in my hand what purported to be a letter head of the Liberal association, and while I was not sure as to who Mr. Stansbury was-and I am not-the letter head says: "Kingston Liberal Association, Bagot and Princess streets, Kingston; A. E. Stansbury, president; J. C. Reynolds, secretary; phone 2423."

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: But if my right hon. friend will permit, he said-

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I am coming to that.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: He said there was a connection with the Frid Construction Company.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Yes, and I am coming to that. I believe that the A. E. Stansbury whose name is at the top of that letter paper is the A. E. Stansbury who made the recommendations referred to in the extracts I have read from Hansard; and I said that if I remembered aright, it was the Frid Construction Company. As q matter of fact, there are three construction companies. There is the Frontenac Construction Company, that came into being in recent years, since this government took office, I am informed. There is the Campbell Construction Company, which came into being in recent years, and there is the Frid Construction Company. I was in error in stating that Mr. Stansbury was president of the Frid Construction Company, but I was not in error in stating that he has
been directing employment with respect to the work at Fort Henry as well as in other places, including the work at Barriefield to which reference has been made in the questions which were asked, although those appointments had to do with more permanent positions. One of them we shall have occasion to discuss when the estimates are under consideration.
The other point that was made was that Mr. Stansbury was the president of the Frid Construction Company. That was entirely erroneous as I find by reference to the papers. I said, "if I remember aright," and I did not remember aright, because there were these three companies. Mr. Stansbury was not the president of the Frid Construction Company, and I do not know what his relations were with respect to either of the other two companies.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: If I may ask, does my right hon. friend believe it is proper to make a statement of that kind upon the basis of fault}' recollection; to have a statement of that kind go out and then have it corrected or denied some days afterwards? Should not these statements be made on the basis of facts?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
It was a correct statement of what is occurring in Kingston and Frontenac with respect to employment. It is there conducted on the basis of politics, purely and simply; men are giving out jobs and using money paid in by the taxpayers, including myself, in order to give employment to one political class and no other. That is what is going on, and one of the men principally responsible for it is Mr. Stansbury, about whom we shall have something to say later when the estimates are under consideration. I do not think the hon. gentleman need have any fear about Mr. Stansbury 'being in any sense, shall I say, libelled or slandered, or that any false impression may be left with respect to him. That need not for one moment engage the hon. gentleman's sympathy or care or worry; I can assure him of that. I think I can say with all certainty from the investigations I have thus far made with respect to the appointments which have been made in connection with these companies that have complete control of these matters, that I have nothing to withdraw; and I say further that it is largely through the work of Mr. Stansbury and one other, whose name we shall mention at the appropriate time, that people who are not willing to subscribe to the tenets of the Liberal party as represented by their association were unable to get

Relief and Agricultural Distress
employment, although they had the same right to it, were just as decent people and had the same claim as Canadians upon employment provided by the money of the taxpayers as had the men whom I have mentioned. I desire to make that abundantly clear, and if there was an error with respect to the position which this gentleman occupies, I greatly regret having made that statement; but it was made with the qualification, " if my recollection is correct," and my recollection was not correct, as I immediately verified when I went to my room, and had the bill not been disposed of I would have made the statement when I returned to the chamber. The hon. gentleman said, very correctly, that he intended to mention it when I was here, but the opportunity did not arise either for him to make the statement or for me to make it before I was called out of the chamber; hence it is that I avail myself of this opportunity on the third reading of this bill, as the minister did when the bill was in committee to make the statement he did.
There is only one point I desire on the third reading of this bill to make abundantly clear. It is that we have reached a stage in this country where I believe common decency necessitates that men should not be compelled to yield such convictions as they may have or such views as they may entertain to a political organization for the purpose of securing employment provided by the money of the taxpayers. For that reason I said the observations of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the other evening were splendid, and I repeat that it was a splendid statement to make. It indicated an earnest desire, I thought, to meet this situation; and if those to whom I have referred-and I say again that Mr. Stansbury, the president of the Liberal association, is one of the principal offenders in that regard-will be governed by the statement made by the Prime Minister that there will be more opportunity for those who have a just claim for employment to find it, and there will be less reason for complaint by the taxpayers that their money is being utilized for the purpose of providing employment only for those who may be politically opposed to them.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I should like to direct attention to some figures which the minister gave at the close of the discussion in committee on this bill. He was referring to the cost of administration, and he read certain figures indicating what that cost had been, according to his information. The figures that he gave struck me as being extraordinarily high, although I was not able to trust my
[Mr. Bennett.J
memory for details as to what were the exact figures. My recollection was that for the first completed year administration for the relief camps cost in the neighbourhood of $80,000; the cost for the following year I thought was $100,000 to $120,000.
I obtained the first volume of the four which were tabled by the minister himself on March 16, 1937. It is called Final Report on the Unemployment Relief Scheme for the Care of Single Homeless Men, administered by the Department of National Defence, 1932-36. I find from this report that the administration, from the inception in October, 1932, to October 31, 1936, for the four years amounted to S489,665, which is rather less than half the figure mentioned by the minister, for one of the years.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: What was that figure, if I might have it again?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
It was $489,665. I
challenged the accuracy of the figure when the minister gave it, and he replied, "That is the cost of the administration staff." So it is quite obvious that in the figures which he gave some other items have been introduced under the heading of administration which were not included in the report which was tabled by the minister. I shall be glad, therefore, if the minister will have inquiries made as to the accuracy of the figures he gave and what items were included to change entirely the figure for the four years given in the report itself.
We are quite accustomed to Liberal speakers presenting arguments against the relief camps. There was quite a volume of Liberal opinion in this country that was not unfavourable to the policy which the previous government was endeavouring to carry out in a time for stress for the care of the single, homeless unemployed, but it was noticeable in the house and in the campaign that Liberals, speaking with partisan motives, were never ready to make any appreciative reference to the work which was undertaken, and no reference is ever made to the work that was accomplished by those men. It was charged that they were not too well treated. It was charged they were improperly working. It was charged they were an unhappy set of people who did little or no work. I who was for a time connected with it know full well that those charges were without foundation, but I think it is of interest to note that, according to that report, the value of the work done by the men in the camps during those four years amounted to $18,213,091.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
Materials, of course, go into that figure, at the price that was paid for them, and labour is accounted for at the going rates; but that is the value of the work of various descriptions which this country has received as a result of the work of those men who were charged with 'being a lazy set of people who never did any work. It is, I think, perfectly right that publicity should be given to that figure, and I think I had better put on Hansard the items which go to make up that total:
Airways, $2,471,698.
Air stations, $2,318,294.
Barracks, $1,474,438.
Clearing of land, $229,632.
Forestry, $1,319,971.
Fortifications and historic sites, $738,518.
Highways, $4,677,173.
Municipal and provincial airports, $175,107.
Rifle ranges, $464,736.
Training camps, $4,343,524.
That makes the total of $18,213,091 which I have already mentioned. That is the work accomplished by men who were cared for at the taxpayers' expense during a time of economic stress, who were sheltered, fed, clothed and medically attended, and many of them, as I know perfectly well, were only too glad to give a certain amount of work in return for what they received. Perhaps the minister will be good enough to take an opportunity to make the two sets of figures fit.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been in session now since the latter part of January, and with the exception of a couple of weeks at the Easter recess we have been on duty continuously. I am trying to sum up the results of our efforts during the time we have been in session. It is no wonder when one goes out from our deliberations here into the country among the people who are interested in our activities, that one finds them amazed . at the little we have accomplished during the last three and a half months.
We find that unemployment is on the increase in our larger industrial areas; that it is becoming an acute problem, more acute now certainly than it was a year ago, and when we ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) for a statement of government policy we are met with practically no reply at all. We were told, for instance, during the previous discussion on this relief measure that we must wait for an announcement of policy until the supplementary estimates are before the house. I would have thought, Mr Speaker, in view of the all-importance of the question of unemployment, that when the
minister was introducing the measure dealing with unemployment and unemployment relief we might have had a statement of policy from the Minister of Labour himself, instead of waiting until the Minister of Finance had brought down his supplementary estimates. But I realize very well how little in the way of policy the government have. In fact, when the supplementary estimates are brought down within the next few weeks it will simply be a case of additional capital expenditures being appropriated to meet an emergency situation. As I have often stated on the floor of the house, no form of capital expenditure is in itself a solution of the problem of unemployment. If capital expenditures could have solved the unemployment problem, certainly it would have been solved in the United States where they have spent billions upon billions of dollars in attempting to deal with the problem. To me, sir, any form of capital expenditure for this purpose is similar to pumping oxygen into a very sick patient. To put into the economic structure of this country more money for capital expenditures will have an effect just so long as the money is in circulation, and the moment the new capital ceases to function we shall revert to the same state of unemployment that we had prior to the pumping of the money into our economic structure.
I would have thought that, having had this problem on our hands for a period of at least eight years, and after realizing, as the Minister of Labour must, that it had not yielded to treatment during that time, that is, to the different forms of capital expenditure and the different forms of relief we have tried, the government would have attempted something new in dealing with the situation. I know the government have great faith in the expansion of trade, and we are all anxious to see trade developed with other countries. I am in favour of trade agreements and of reducing tariffs, but I realize more and more as the years go by that a reduction of our tariffs and the creation of more trade agreements between ourselves and other parts of the world are in themselves no solution of the problems of the day. We are attempting now to effect another trade agreement between the United States and ourselves, but does it not seem absurd on the face of it to expect that because we effect a trade agreement with the United States, which has a more serious unemployment than we have, we are going to improve materially conditions in Canada? Trade agreements, in fact, while they might expand trade in one direction, very often have the effect

Relief and Agricultural Distress
of strangling trade in other directions, and it often happens that the result of trade agreements which are effected is merely to create, new channels of trade without creating imuch additional trade; in other words, the sum total of benefits created is not very much.
As I said a moment ago, we are now in the second half of the session of parliament; perhaps we shall not sit as long as we have already done, and I think we should at least have a definite statement of policy from the government as to what they intend doing about the unemployment situation. We have in this country to-day at least 400,000 men and women who are out of work, and I am just wondering what hope this session of parliament is going to give to this vast number of men and women who are out of work, and who are looking to parliament for the solution of their problems and difficulties. There is nothing we have done during the past three months to give one ray of hope to this vast number of unemployed in this dominion, and is it any wonder that they are beginning to look on us with a certain mark of indifference, and some with a good deal of skepticism as to whether we really mean business in our attempts to solve this particular problem?
Wherever I go these days the same question is put to me:	What is parliament doing
to meet the problems confronting us in the dominion at the present time? And what answer can I give? There is only one answer, and that is that we are doing very little; that we are continuing to go along in exactly the same way as we have done during the past eight years. I put it to the hon. Minister of Labour, a student of economics, which is a form of science:	If, after eight years
the very serious problem of unemployment has not yielded to the treatment we have been giving it, is it not the logical thing, is it not the scientific thing, that we should seek to apply new remedies to meet existing conditions? Yet there are no new remedies; there is nothing new. -We are continuing for the ensuing year with exactly the same kind of thing we have had in effect for the last seven or eight years. In 1930 we passed a bill dealing with public works and the giving of unemployment relief in the way of food, clothing and shelter. Now, eight years after we had our first serious problem of unemployment to cope with, we are dealing with it in exactly the same way. There is nothing scientific; I do not think there is anything really Liberal, about that method of dealing with unemployment. I had hoped that this

year, when we met in January, faced with a falling volume of trade, the government would have presented some other means of dealing with the situation.
The present government have been rather fortunate. They came into power on the crest of a wave of trade expansion. When they went out of office in 1930, trade was on the decline. The moment contraction again sets in, we are faced with the same problem which confronted us in 1930, but with no means provided by the government, at any rate no means that they have brought before the house, in the way of an attempt to do something effective to meet the situation. How ineffective the house seems to be, particularly at this session! For the past three or four days we have been listening to a discussion on the reduction of the tariff upon implements of farm production. I am favourable to such a reduction. But does it not seem incongruous to have Liberal members pleading with a Liberal government to put a Liberal plank into effect by way of legislation? It should not require three or four days' discussion in the house to convince the government of the necessity of putting their own platform into effect. It could have been done in the first session of this parliament-

speechtext: And it was.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
-if the government had
wanted to do so. But of course we had a lengthy inquiry by one of our committees, and then several days' discussion a year after the report was presented. Probably, when the next budget comes down or when the last budget before the next election is presented, we may find a little relief to the farmer by way of reduction in the tariff on farm implements. What I am more interested in is to make this parliament an instrument of some benefit and value to the great masses of our people. When I look at this session I find it is one of the most barren we have had in the history of this chamber. From the end of January to the present time we have not passed anything that can really be called legislation. As regards the present bill, it is not really new legislation, it is merely continuing legislation which we have had for the past seven or eight years. The other legislation which we were promised at the beginning of the session is likely to go into the discard; I refer particularly to the matter of unemployment insurance. So we have now been in session for approximately three and a half months; if we are asked what we have done in that time we can only say that nothing has been done, and as a person put

Relief and Agricultural Distress
it to me the other night, we have done it as effectively as any one knows how it can be done.
My plea to the government at this time is to face the situation in the serious way in which I expect a government to deal with so grave a question. Otherwise, when the session is over, what shall we be able to show? Money again allotted for unemployment and farm relief. As I have repeated until I am tired of saying it, I do not want to see our hundreds of thousands of unemployed kept on relief; I would far sooner put them in a position where they could earn their livelihood and retain their self-respect. It may be that a limited amount of funds will be put into the deferred estimates for public relief work. I am anxious to alleviate unemployment to the fullest extent we possibly can; but may I again point out that no form of public works is in itself any more than a palliative, and very often only a poor one at that. I would plead with the minister, with all the strength and earnestness of which I am capable, to devise some further ways and means of dealing with unemployment, dealing with it as effectively as they are trying to do in other parts of the world. To the south of us the president, in spite of drawbacks and handicaps, is at least making efforts to deal with this recurring question. Although he has spent billions of dollars, he has also taken other means of coping with the problem. But here we sit still. Week by week we sit idly by. Month after month goes by, but we accomplish so little and give so little encouragement to the unemployed. Now that we are on the third reading of this bill, I trust that before the session closes we shall have some announcement from the minister on behalf of the government that they are going to take means entirely different from those adopted in the past in order to cope with the present problem which has been with us in an acute form for the last eight years.

a $2,000,000 government financed summer-fallow program to follow up on the heels of the spring seed and feed distribution.

As I have said, the hon. member has already made three speeches on this matter, one at the proper time and two at times when the rules of the house prevented him from making a speech. Well, I shall put it in this way, that under this act there is power for the minister to make arrangements with a government to relieve agricultural distress. The premier of Saskatchewan has announced a program of that kind. That program could not be announced unless some arrangements had been made with this government, for the finances of that province will not permit a two million dollar expenditure on summer-fallow or anything else without the approval of this government. I submit, therefore, if an arrangement of that kind has already been

Relief and Agricultural Distress
made, that we should have a statement from the minister which might come under any of the provisions of this bill. It is a very bold statement, particularly at this time. I quote:
Depending upon the date of the election, the summer-fallow program would have to be financed either before or after the election, the premier continued. "If it is after the election," the premier continued, "ask yourself who can provide aid for you better, a government that has maintained the province's credit or one that contends that maintaining credit doesn't matter."
There is no question, in view of this statement, that some arrangement has been made between the two governments with respect to assisting farmers with their summer-fallow. It is right that they should be assisted, but we should have a statement now on the third reading of the bill as to what arrangement has been made in that respect with the province of Saskatchewan.

speechtext:
The fact is that when we contemplate conditions here at the present time, in the light of the fact that a large portion of our agricultural area has been out of production for five years, we have every reason for confidence instead of despair. I say to my hon. friend in all kindness that the group to which he belongs was born in depression and nourished in despair. My hon. friend has not been willing to admit that there has been a distinct improvement from time to time. I have given the house on various occasions evidence of improvement in large sections of the country. In the maritime provinces in the past two years, unemployment, so far as it has affected relief, has been reduced 75 per cent; in the two central provinces the number of those on relief has been reduced between 35 and 40 per cent; in British Columbia there has been a reduction of 35 per cent. Only in the western provinces where climatic disturbances have had their effect, putting a large area out of production, has there been the persistent condition in an aggravated form that causes concern to my hon. friend. And let me assure him that he is not alone in that concern. Certainly this government, since it came to office, has not shown any indifference towards that problem.
My hon. friend says that we have not found a solution. Can he point to a single country that has found a solution except on the basis of forced labour, regimentation, and the enlisting of men in armies, and does he favour such methods?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
There is no comparison
between this country and New Zealand. My hon. friend is going far afield. He began with a country in which the conditions are similar to ours, the United States, and now he is going to New Zealand. The truth of the matter is that we have not at any time shown any lack of interest or desire to deal with the problem. We have proceeded not on one line, but on several lines. We have tried to profit by the experience of our predecessors and have endeavoured to branch out along some lines of our own. We did not, as some hon. members have suggested, believe that foreign markets had disappeared for all time. We had the courage of our faith and we went out to find foreign markets; and the Prime Minister on Armistice day found a great market to the south that had not been enjoyed under treaty by this countiy since 1866. What is more, we believe that this market will be extended in time to come. We have gone in other directions as well and have found markets which my hon. friends said were beyond resurrection. We have found those markets and we have the faith that we can proceed along that line constructively and successfully.
As for relief works, I have Stated on many occasions that relief works as such are not more than a palliative; there is no difference between my hon. friend and myself in that regard. We have, however, tried to concentrate expenditures in directions where there will be an increase in collateral and ultimate employment, and we believe that we should make expenditures in that direction where possible. The hon. gentleman comes from the great city of Winnipeg, and he knows that as a result of assistance given by this government and by the preceding administration there has been established there a modern sewage disposal plant which surely was of benefit to that community, and of temporary benefit to thousands of unemployed in Winnipeg. We have, through assistance given in connection with highways, opened up new areas and given encouragement to the mining industry, to the tourist trade, and to forestry; and in these directions, surely, our expenditures have not been wasteful. They have
provided immediate employment, and also assisted towards greater ultimate employment.
We have also dealt with relief settlement on a moderate scale, and here again my hon. friend was the first to say that in the direction of rural rehabilitation we should proceed gradually and surely, because in the experience of some of the provinces we have found that to take families from the city and place them on the land tended to make their condition worse rather than improve it. We have, however, proceeded in that direction in association with certain provinces, and in some cases we have made marked progress in rural reestablishment.
We have also initiated plans for training the youth of Canada for reestablishment in industry. When that vote was before this house last year it was said to be an experimental vote. We wished to find our way, and we still wish to proceed cautiously, but surely. I think my hon. friend would not suggest for a moment that moving in that direction is against the interests of this country or of the unemployed young people who have not been able to find positions for themselves in recent years. Surely, if my hon. friend examines the estimates of last year, as he will in due course examine the estimates of this year, he will find that we have not proceeded along one line only, with any thought that in any one policy is to be found a solution for unemployment. That would be contrary to the experience of all other countries. But we have proceeded along a number of lines, trying to improve the situation in several directions at the same time, and we believe that our policies have had due effect.
I am just reminded of what has been done under the home improvement plan, also the Dominion Housing Act with its altered regulations; some $30,000,000 worth of construction has been stimulated under that legislation. Is that not a movement in the right direction, and does it not show the wisdom of government seeking when necessary to stimulate the operations of private industry to give employment in this country?
These are the directions along which this government has moved. If our progress has not been spectacular, at least it has been sustained. I have already given indications at various times of the improvement which has taken place despite the fact that in this great agricultural country there has been a large area out of production. I am not prepared to give a final answer as to our power to deal with unemployment until our agricultural provinces are restored to something

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: The change in section 1 arises out of the suggestions made in committee. It was suggested that paragraph (d) as drafted in the original bill should be further amended to include agreements for sale and assignments of such agreements in connection with which privity of contract was lacking. It will be remembered that section 1 as originally devised was intended to provide for cases where absence of privity of contract had hitherto debarred consideration by boards of review of contracts in connection with cases coming before them. The one suggestion which came from members of the committee and which seemed to find general acceptance was that the principle should be extended to include agreements of sale, and this is provided for in the section as amended.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think there are some objectionable features in the amendment. As the minister has stated, the original measure as drafted and as interpreted by judges and those to whom it was referred was held not to include a person who had acquired property subject to encumbrance. The whole basis of the act is the insolvency of the farmer and the arrangement of his debts. The decision went on the basis that there was no privity of contract; that there was no debt existing between a person who had purchased a farm subject to mortgage, and the holder of that mortgage. That principle is absolutely sound. The holder of that mortgage could not sue the party who had purchased the farm subject to mortgage. There was no action against him directly, because there was no covenant between the parties. All that could be done was to foreclose the mortgage. There was no liability whatsoever on the purchaser in respect of the mortgage. And no matter what that purchaser might be worth; no matter what other property he might have, or no
matter what other assets he might have- there might be money in the bank, or an indication of solvency in many respects- the holder of that mortgage had no remedy whatever before the act was passed. The whole intention of the act was to enable the party indebted to the other to have a compromise of his debts. It seems to me that it is extending the act far beyond its original seoipe and intention and, as I pointed out before, it is introducing further complications and further difficulties at a time when the difficulties ought to be contracted. It seems to me we are entering upon another field upon which we should not enter at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: The remarks of the hon. member revert to the discussion which took place previously with respect to the principle involved. I do not think I can add anything to what was said on that occasion. Certainly at the present time there are about 3,000 cases of farmers which cannot be dealt with by boards of review, because of the absence of privity of contract. I gathered it to be the sense of the house that the greatest good for the greatest number would be served by refusing further to allow 'the lack of privity of contract to prevent the board from considering the actual case. I have not any doubt that, headed as each board is by a judge of the high court, the circumstances involved with respect to the original vendor and the original purchaser will, of course, be fully considered. I hesitate to propose anything which would deprive anyone of any right; but, after all, this is bankruptcy legislation, and we must never lose sight of that fact. I therefore believe it to be the sense of the committee that the section pass.
Section agreed to.

Section 2 of the bill, relating to the estates of deceased farmers, contains only two changes; only two changes have been made since the original bill was before the committee. One change is the insertion of the words "occurring on or after the 3rd day of July, 1934," after the word "farmer" in the first line, as a result of which the benefits under the amendment will be applicable only to the estates of farmers who died after the original act was passed. It is thought well not to extend the privilege beyond the coming into force of the original act. In every other such case the amendment stands exactly as when it appeared before the committee on the previous occasion, and
Farmers' Creditors Act

provides that the estates of deceased farmers may go before a receiver under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and later before a board of review, suggesting an arrangement or composition upon the conditions set out in subsection 2. That subsection reads:
The court, upon being satisfied that a member of the family of the decedent resides and will continue to reside upon the farm of the decedent and intends and is able to operate the same may, ex parte, upon such terms and conditions as the court deems fit, by order, grant such application.
When the bill was before the committee previously, the suggestion was made by the hon. member for Rosthern and, I believe, also by the leader of the opposition, that the proceedings should be ex parte, in order to make them as inexpensive as possible upon the debtor. But it will be noticed that the principle of the act is maintained, namely the principle of enabling the farmer to continue on the farm. If a member of the family of a deceased farmer demonstrates to the satisfaction of the court his or her intention or ability to remain upon and to operate the farm, then the executors of the estate of the farmer have the same rights, under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, as the farmer would have had had he continued to live.

The board will take all those factors into account. We cannot make a judicial decision in this committee as to what would happen in a particular case. We can only provide adequate and fair judicial machinery to take into account the circumstances of each individual case.
I would remind my hon. friend that I did not create this legislation; I inherited it. My hon. friend had a very great deal more to do with its inception than I had. All these exceptional cases must have been in the minds of those who framed the act, with the best motives in the world, and how did they solve them? They did it as far as possible by setting up a tribunal which would exercise judgment in the circumstances of the individual cases. In all these amendments I am endeavouring to follow that principle fully,
and to apply to cases where privity of contract up to the present has barred consideration by the board the same principles that have applied in all other cases. That has been the object, and I think the draughtsmen have carried it out very well. But if any member of this committee asks me what will happen in this or that kind of case, I am afraid I can give only the answer I would give if I were asked what would happen in court under certain circumstances. I would simply say that the judge would have to assess the various factors entering into the matter, size them up and give his decision. I submit that here we cannot enter into the judicial aspects of the cases which may come before the boards.

It was passed in 1934, I think, and we are now in 1938. I have been endeavouring to convince the minister that instead of expanding it he should wipe it out, according to the original intention and purpose of the act. We are told that conditions are improved and that everything is so much better. When I point out to the minister that the only debts which can be taken into consideration are those that were in existence at the time the act was passed, and that four years have gone by since then, surely there is not the same reason for continuing the act that there was for initiating the act. The debts that existed in 1934 must have been dealt with in the main in some way by this time, and to expand the act now and to introduce all these added complications is, I submit, contrary to the original intention and purpose. It is going to end in confusion and create complications.
As has been pointed out, in the operation of the act in Ontario the hardship now is not so much upon the farmer as upon the party who holds a farm mortgage. About eighty per cent of these are farmers who have loaned money to other farmers, neighbours who have loaned to neighbours, persons who have sold their farms and taken back mortgages. The hardship is upon them, and that hardship is just as great as that of the farmer. It seems
Farmers' Creditors Act

to me that the farmers cannot complain, after a lapse of four years, if legislation of this kind should, at least, not be expanded. It should be repealed. All I wish to urge is that in Ontario, in any case, the minister, as I believe he has taken power under this act, will see that it is repealed, and I suggest that the first day of July would be a suitable date for that repeal. I proposed to introduce a bill for that purpose. If the minister could only give me the assurance, which I am sure he will not, that this is his intention in connection with Ontario, I would not quarrel or quibble about some of the provisions that go in the direction of expanding the operation of the act, and talcing it, as I think, beyond its original intention and scope, with further difficulties and complications and a greater measure of hardship, after this lapse of time, than the minister is going to relieve.

My hon. friend always treats me with such courtesy that I hesitate to differ with him, at least in any acrimonious way. It is difficult for me to add anything to what was said in the discussion on the second reading and in the committee proceedings before on this bill. The point which my hon. friend now raises is one, I submit, which was settled by the house when it adopted the second reading of the bill. There was no doubt, as a result of the full discussion, what the will of the house generally was as to the principles contained in this amending measure. May I point out in that connection that I was very frank with the house and said quite plainly that, as a result of the discussion in previous sessions, I was quite certain I could not get through the house the amendments which were regarded as necessary by the representatives of some of the provinces unless I could also incorporate in the bill a provision which would permit of the termination of the operation of the act in some provinces. That provision is in the bill. I know it is a lot to ask of my hon. friend; but with respect to when the termination will take place in this province or that, I am afraid that, hard though it may be, he will have to trust the government. I know that is all but impossible for him to do; 'but I think he knows my views on the matter and that I do not desire to keep the act in operation in any province in which it is clear it is doing more harm than good.
My hon. friend and a number of others have undertaken to demonstrate in connection with various provinces that the act is now doing more harm than good. I am prepared to consider such representations at any time and will give fair consideration to

them in any recommendations I make to my colleagues in the government with regard to putting into force the section withdrawing the provisions of the act from operation in any particular province. I desire to make quite clear, however, that the government believes there are several provinces in which this act continues to perform at the present time, a necessary service for the farmers, and in which under no consideration at the present time would we consider withdrawing its operation. On the other hand, there are provinces in which the evidence accumulates that the act is doing the farmer more harm than good. In such cases we are prepared to act on the powers which are contained in a section which is not yet before the committee but which was very thoroughly discussed on a former occasion.
